entities.summary:
Girolamo Verallo (1497–1555) was an Italian Roman Catholic cardinal and papal diplomat.

As the papal legate to the Holy Roman Empire, he played a crucial role in the Trent Council (1545–1563), which aimed to reform the Church's doctrine on sacraments and clerical celibacy. His diplomatic efforts helped maintain the fragile peace between the Protestant Reformation and Catholicism during this tumultuous period.

Verallo's legacy extends beyond his diplomatic accomplishments, as he was a key figure in shaping the Counter-Reformation policies of Pope Paul IV (1555–1559). His contributions to the Church's reform efforts had far-reaching consequences, influencing the development of Catholic theology and practice for centuries to come.

The significance of Verallo's life and work can be seen in the enduring impact of his diplomatic efforts on European politics and religion during the 16th century. Despite limited access to primary sources, it is clear that Verallo's actions played a significant role in maintaining stability in a time of great upheaval.

The 1555 papal conclave produced no new pope, as the College of Cardinals deadlocked over the election of Pope Pius IV (1559–1565), who succeeded Paul IV.
